implementation_notes: .NET absorbed this pattern into the platform: ClaimsPrincipal (an IPrincipal) is the descriptor, carrying one or more ClaimsIdentity instances whose Claim objects are the security-relevant attributes, and ASP.NET Core populates HttpContext.User per request from the authentication middleware. Consumers ask User.FindFirstValue(...) or User.IsInRole("Admin") instead of parsing tokens; ClaimsPrincipal.Current still exists for compatibility but resolves through ClaimsPrincipalSelector/Thread.CurrentPrincipal. Write a custom descriptor only when domain attributes need provenance or typing that claims do not model - and then wrap the principal instead of creating a second source of truth.
pitfalls: ClaimsPrincipal.Current is ambient (thread and async-local) and unreliable in ASP.NET Core; read HttpContext.User or inject IHttpContextAccessor instead of the static property.

Identity.Name and ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier are different claims: code that assumes the primary identity's name is the subject id breaks with issuers that only provide "sub", and claim names must be mapped per issuer.

Claims are strings: IsInRole depends on the ClaimsIdentity's RoleClaimType (ClaimTypes.Role by default), so an identity provider that emits "roles" needs an explicit mapping or the check silently fails.
